1.reasoning: In Genesis 1:6-8 the firmament was made to separate the waters above from the waters below. None of the three printed options (light source, soil erosion, body temperature) states this; light is the purpose of the luminaries on day four, not the firmament.
1.issue: Only options A-C present and none is correct; option D (presumably 'separate the waters') appears to be missing from the transcription.

2.reasoning: Genesis 2:17: 'in the day that you eat of it you shall die.' The stated reason for the prohibition was death. 'Exposure to evil' is defensible from the tree's name, but the text names death as the consequence.
2.issue: B (exposure to evil) is arguable on a theological reading.

3.reasoning: Genesis 1:28: God blessed man and woman, saying 'be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it.' Animals were told to multiply but were not given dominion to subdue the earth.

4.reasoning: Joseph advised that a fifth of the produce be stored during the seven years of plenty, and this was done (Genesis 41:34-49). The butler's restoration came earlier, from interpreting his own dream.

5.reasoning: Joseph foresaw the coming famine and planned ahead for it, which shows foresight (visionary). Righteousness is a general trait of Joseph's but is not what the interpretation and advice show.

6.reasoning: Moses killed the Egyptian he saw beating a Hebrew, 'one of his people' (Exodus 2:11-12). This shows loyalty to his Hebrew roots. He was not acting on God's command then, so D does not fit.

7.reasoning: Numbers 13:31: ten of the twelve spies gave this report, while Joshua and Caleb disagreed. So it was the majority view, not the view of all the spies.
7.issue: 'spics' is a typo for 'spies'; 'able to up' is missing 'go'.

8.reasoning: Numbers 27:18-20: God told Moses to lay his hand on Joshua and invest him with some of his authority so that the congregation would obey him. Eleazar only took part in the commissioning.

9.reasoning: Joshua 1:8: 'This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night... then you shall have good success.'

10.reasoning: Barak would only go to battle if Deborah went with him (Judges 4:8). Her agreeing to lead Israel to war against Sisera showed courage and leadership. The other pairs do not describe going into battle.

11.reasoning: Judges 4:1-3: Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, so God sold them into the hand of Jabin of Canaan, who oppressed them for twenty years. The oppression punished unfaithfulness, which shows God expects obedience. C is close but is worded as a general right, not the reason.

12.reasoning: 1 Samuel 2:25 says they would not listen to their father 'for it was the will of the Lord to slay them.' The text gives this reason directly.

13.reasoning: 1 Samuel 8:5: 'Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways; now appoint for us a king.' D, a king to fight their battles like the other nations (8:20), is a secondary reason given later.
13.issue: D is partly defensible from 1 Samuel 8:20.

14.reasoning: Saul said this on Mount Gilboa while fighting the Philistines (1 Samuel 31:4). In Samuel, 'uncircumcised' is the standard term for the Philistines.

15.reasoning: 1 Samuel 26:12: they were all asleep 'because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.'

16.reasoning: 2 Samuel 12:18: 'How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm.' The servants did not fear being harmed themselves.

17.reasoning: 1 Kings 11:1-10: Solomon loved many foreign women from nations God had forbidden Israel to marry into, and they turned his heart to other gods.

18.reasoning: 1 Kings 12:3-4: Jeroboam and the assembly of Israel came to Rehoboam at Shechem and asked him to lighten the heavy yoke. The installation was at Shechem, not Gibeon, and the break-away came after Rehoboam refused.

19.reasoning: 1 Kings 3:14: 'If you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes... then I will lengthen your days.'

20.reasoning: Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, saying Baal might be musing or gone aside (1 Kings 18:27).

21.reasoning: Because of Ahab's idolatry, Elijah announced there would be no dew or rain (1 Kings 17:1), and a three-year drought followed.

22.reasoning: The letters arranged a fast and false witnesses so that Naboth would be condemned under the law, which cleared the way for Ahab to take the vineyard (1 Kings 21:8-16). Stoning (C) was the means she ordered, but her aim was the vineyard under a show of legality.
22.issue: C describes what the letters ordered and is arguable.

23.reasoning: 2 Kings 5:7: the king of Israel read the Syrian king's letter, tore his clothes and said this.

24.reasoning: 2 Kings 22:11: when the king heard the words of the book of the law, he rent his clothes. Only after that did he send to inquire of the Lord, and the purge of idols came later.

25.reasoning: 2 Kings 22:19-20: because Josiah was penitent, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and his eyes would not see the evil coming on the place. He actually died in battle at Megiddo.
25.issue: Option says 'Isreal's' where the text is about Judah/Jerusalem; answer unaffected.

26.reasoning: Nehemiah 2:17: 'Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer be a reproach' (RSV 'disgrace'). 'Challenge' fits how he responded, but the text calls the ruins a reproach.

27.reasoning: 2 Kings 24:14 and 25:12: none remained except the poorest people of the land, who were left as vinedressers and ploughmen.

28.reasoning: Daniel 3:13: Nebuchadnezzar, in furious rage, commanded that the three be brought. He questioned them and only then ordered the furnace.

29.reasoning: Amos 7:10-13: Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, told Amos not to prophesy there because 'it is the king's sanctuary.' Jeroboam II was the king he reported to.

30.reasoning: Amos 4:2-3 pictures the people dragged away with hooks, like captives led off by their captors. It predicts exile and subjugation, not fishing or scattering.

31.reasoning: Jesus, who was sinless, submitted to John's baptism 'to fulfil all righteousness' (Matthew 3:13-15). This shows humility. John's reluctance was about his own unworthiness.

32.reasoning: Matthew 4:5-6: on the pinnacle of the temple the devil said, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.' Invoking the angels was the supporting quotation, not the challenge itself.

33.reasoning: After the miraculous catch (Luke 5:8), Peter's sense of his own sinfulness in Jesus' presence shows he saw the holy and divine in him. 'Authority' is arguable but weaker.

34.reasoning: Jesus' demands of discipleship, such as denying oneself, taking up the cross and counting the cost (Luke 9:23, 14:25-33), teach self-denial and determination.

35.reasoning: The master jailed him because he showed no mercy to his fellow servant after being forgiven himself (Matthew 18:32-34). The debt (C) was the terms of his jailing, but his harsh treatment of the fellow servant was why he was jailed.
35.issue: C is arguable, since he was jailed until he paid the debt.

36.reasoning: Matthew 6:14 and Luke 6:37: if you forgive others, your heavenly Father will forgive you, so they obtain pardon. 'See God' and 'sons of God' belong to other Beatitudes.

37.reasoning: Matthew 26:38, 41: 'Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation', which is a call to be vigilant.

38.reasoning: Matthew 26:63: 'I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.' The claim about destroying the temple came from the witnesses, not Caiaphas's question.

39.reasoning: On the Emmaus road, Jesus rebuked them for being slow to believe what the prophets had said, and explained that the Christ had to suffer (Luke 24:25-27). The lesson is that God's word must be fulfilled.
39.issue: Stem is garbled: it was Jesus who rebuked Cleopas and his companion, not Cleopas who rebuked Jesus; 'reference' probably means 'inference'.

40.reasoning: Matthew 27:51 lists, in order: the temple curtain was torn in two, then the earth shook, the rocks split, and the tombs were opened.

41.reasoning: Acts 5:4-5: Peter said this to Ananias, and when Ananias heard these words he fell down and died. Sapphira's death came about three hours later.

42.reasoning: Acts 6:1-3: the Hellenists complained that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution, so the seven were appointed. The growing number of disciples was the background, not the direct reason.

43.reasoning: Peter explained that God had shown him no one is unclean and that God gave the Gentiles the same gift (Acts 11:1-18). Christians should therefore treat all people equally.

44.reasoning: After Pentecost the apostles preached boldly (Acts 2), the church was born, about three thousand accepted Jesus as Christ, and evangelism began. Fear is the opposite of the outcome.

45.reasoning: Acts 9:15-16: Saul was a chosen instrument to carry Christ's name, and 'I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.'

46.reasoning: James 2:8 defines the royal law as 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself.' That corresponds to being each other's keeper. 'Do good to those who hate them' is love of enemies, a different command.

47.reasoning: James 5:13-14: 'Is any among you suffering? Let him pray.' The elders are called for the sick.

48.reasoning: 1 Peter 2:2: 'Like newborn babes, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up to salvation.'

49.reasoning: 1 Peter 5:5: 'Likewise you that are younger be subject to the elders.'

50.reasoning: 1 Peter 5:10 and 4:13: after you have suffered a little while, the God who called you to his eternal glory will restore you, so suffering is temporary and leads to glory. A is also Petrine (1 Peter 2:21, 4:1), which makes it defensible.
50.issue: A (Christ also suffered) is defensible from 1 Peter 2:21.
